query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, exposure to oxidizing (or strongly reducing) high-temperature environments promotes selective oxidation (or deoxidation) of reactive elements (notably Ti and Cr) at matrix and grain-boundary regions. This leads to the formation of brittle secondary oxide or phase precipitates and local compositional depletion, which in turn alters the stacking fault energy and triggers an unfavorable phase transition (e.g., from the ductile FCC to a more brittle BCC or intermetallic phase). The resulting microstructural degradation (e.g., weakened matrix/cohesion at interfaces) accumulates stress concentrations that eventually cause catastrophic failure under mechanical load.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured HEA with a supersaturated solid solution FCC matrix containing fine secondary phases introduced during processing.
generation.intervention: Systematically control the gas environment during elevated-temperature exposure by comparing oxidizing atmospheres (with elevated oxygen partial pressure) to reducing atmospheres (with low oxygen levels).
generation.conditions: Temperature range where oxidation/reduction kinetics are active (e.g., 700–1000 °C) and exposure durations long enough to allow significant scale or phase evolution, under controlled gas chemistries.
generation.structural_mediator: Selective oxidation-induced formation of brittle oxide precipitates and compositional depletion zones at grain boundaries and within the matrix, which modify local dislocation behavior and phase stability.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, reactive elements such as Ti and Cr preferentially form oxide phases at interfaces. This creates localized depletion in the surrounding FCC matrix, leading to a reduction in ductility by lowering the stacking fault energy and facilitating an FCC-to-brittle phase (e.g., BCC or intermetallic) transition. Under reducing conditions, the absence of such oxidation maintains the metastable ductile microstructure. The embrittlement and subsequent degradation of mechanical integrity set up conditions for catastrophic failure in service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed in oxidizing environments will develop intergranular oxide layers and secondary brittle phases, leading to a measurable decrease in ductility and creep/tensile performance relative to the as-built baseline. In contrast, samples in a reducing atmosphere will show limited or delayed degradation. The transition from ductile FCC to a brittle secondary phase is expected to correlate with the onset of catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: The as-built state of the HEA, exhibiting a ductile FCC matrix with fine secondary phases and relatively high strength and ductility at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–1000 °C) and in gas environments where oxygen activity (or reducing species) is sufficiently high to drive selective oxidation or deoxidation kinetics. Deviations in gas composition outside these boundaries may not produce the predicted phase transitions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxidation and phase transformation, the critical oxide layer thickness for embrittlement, and the exact nature of the phase transition (e.g., FCC-to-BCC vs intermetallic formation) have uncertainties that require further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples and subject them to elevated-temperature (e.g., 800 °C) exposures for fixed durations in atmospheres with controlled oxygen partial pressures ranging from oxidizing to reducing. Post-exposure, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, XRD, and chemical mapping) and mechanical testing (tensile tests, creep tests). Compare the development of oxide or secondary brittle phases and changes in mechanical performance.
measurements: Quantitative phase analysis (XRD) to detect the presence and extent of any secondary phases (oxides, BCC, or intermetallic phases).
Chemical composition mapping (EDS/TEM) at grain boundaries and matrix regions to assess depletion or enrichment of Ti and Cr.
Mechanical property measurements (tensile strength, ductility, creep rates) relative to the as-built state.
Fractography to identify the mode of failure and presence of embrittling intergranular oxide layers.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in phase composition (i.e., absence of additional brittle phases or oxide scales) or mechanical degradation (retaining ductility/strength similar to the as-built state) is observed between samples exposed in oxidizing vs reducing environments, or if catastrophic failure does not correlate with the presence of oxidation-induced microstructural changes, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy

Abstract: AbstractThis article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. Corrosion and Thermal Stability of CrMnFeNi High Entropy Alloy in Molten FLiBe Salt

Abstract: AbstractThe corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Mechanisms of chemical-reaction-induced tensile deformation of an Fe/Ni/Cr alloy revealed by reactive atomistic simulations†

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries.
